subject: Mathematics
title: Collecting School Survey Data
hook: Raj and Meera survey classmates to learn how to collect and display data.

slides.title: The Survey
slides.storyContext: Raj asks classmates: 'What is your favorite subject?' Meera organizes the answers: Math (8), Science (6), English (4), Hindi (5), Sports (7).
slides.inSimpleWords: Data is information we collect and organize.

image.alt: The Survey — Data Handling and Presentation

slides.title: What is Data?

points.label: Definition
points.text: Data is facts and figures collected through observation, measurement, or surveys.

points.label: Examples
points.text: Heights of students, favorite colors, test scores, number of books read.

slides.inSimpleWords: Data tells us about the world using numbers and facts.

slides.title: Collecting Data
slides.storyContext: Meera explains: data can come from surveys, observations, or measurements. Always ask clear questions.

points.label: Types of Data
points.text: Qualitative (colors, preferences), Quantitative (numbers, measurements).

slides.inSimpleWords: Data is facts and information collected carefully.

image.alt: Collecting Data — Data Handling and Presentation

slides.title: Survey Question Example

example.problem: Write a clear survey question to collect favorite sports from 25 classmates.
example.solution: Bad: 'Do you like sports?' Good: 'Which sport do you like best: Cricket, Football, Basketball, Badminton, or Tennis?' Clear options make data easier to collect.

slides.inSimpleWords: Good survey questions have clear choices and no confusing words.

slides.title: The Counting Begins
slides.storyContext: Raj pulls out tally marks. 'One for Math... two for Math... Meera, your turn to count Science votes!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Tallying tracks data as it comes in.

slides.title: Tally Marks System

points.label: Single Mark
points.text: One mark = one vote: |

points.label: Group of Five
points.text: Five marks in a group: ||||/

points.label: Counting
points.text: Makes it easy to count to 5, then 10, then 15...

slides.inSimpleWords: Tally marks are quick and help count to five.

slides.title: Tallying and Frequency
slides.storyContext: Raj uses tally marks to count: Math |||||| || (8 votes), Science |||| | (6 votes).

example.problem: Make a frequency table for favorite colors: Red (7), Blue (9), Green (5), Yellow (4).
example.solution:
Color | Tally | Frequency
Red | |||||| | 7
Blue | |||||||| | 9
Green | ||||| | 5
Yellow | |||| | 4

slides.inSimpleWords: Tally marks and frequency tables organize counted data.

image.alt: Tallying and Frequency — Data Handling and Presentation

slides.title: Organizing the Results
slides.storyContext: Raj and Meera sit together after the survey. Meera says, 'Now let's put this in order: first count, then table, then a picture everyone can read.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Once we collect data, we arrange it step by step.

slides.title: Frequency Table

points.label: What it is
points.text: A table listing each item and how many times it appears (its frequency).

points.label: How to use
points.text: Count tally marks for each category. Sum the tallies to get frequency.

slides.inSimpleWords: A frequency table shows what and how many.

slides.title: Building a Frequency Table

example.problem: Students were asked 'What breakfast do you eat?' Tally: Idli 9, Dosa 7, Upma 5, Paratha 4. Create a frequency table.
example.solution:
Breakfast | Tally | Frequency
Idli | ||||||||| | 9
Dosa | ||||||| | 7
Upma | ||||| | 5
Paratha | |||| | 4

slides.inSimpleWords: Write the item name, draw tallies, count the tallies for frequency.

slides.title: Time to Draw
slides.storyContext: Meera pulls out colored pencils. 'Raj, let's make a picture of our data. A chart anyone can understand at a glance!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Charts and pictures tell data stories visually.

slides.title: Pictographs and Bar Charts
slides.storyContext: Meera draws a bar chart: each bar's height shows how many votes each subject got.

points.label: Pictograph
points.text: Uses pictures to represent data; 1 picture = a fixed number of items.

points.label: Bar Chart
points.text: Uses rectangular bars to compare quantities across categories.

slides.inSimpleWords: Charts make data easy to see and compare at a glance.

image.alt: Pictographs and Bar Charts — Data Handling and Presentation

slides.title: Reading a Pictograph

example.problem: A pictograph shows favorite fruits: Apple (3 🍎), Mango (4 🥭), Banana (2 🍌). Each symbol = 2 students. How many students like mango?
example.solution: 4 symbols × 2 students per symbol = 8 students like mango.

slides.inSimpleWords: Count the pictures and multiply by the 'value per picture'.

slides.title: Making a Bar Chart
slides.storyContext: Raj draws the favorite subject bar chart: y-axis = number of votes (0-8), x-axis = subjects.

example.problem: Draw a bar chart for favorite sport: Cricket (10), Football (8), Basketball (6), Tennis (4).
example.solution: Bars rise to 10, 8, 6, 4 respectively. Cricket has the tallest bar, tennis the shortest.

slides.inSimpleWords: Height of bar = amount of data for that category.

image.alt: Making a Bar Chart — Data Handling and Presentation

slides.title: Analyzing the Data
slides.storyContext: Meera looks at their chart and asks, 'What number is in the middle? Which subject appears most often? What's the average?'
slides.inSimpleWords: Once we display data, we can find patterns and meaning.

slides.title: Mean, Median, Mode
slides.storyContext: Meera analyzes the vote numbers: Mean (average), Median (middle), Mode (most common).

points.label: Mean
points.text: Sum of all values ÷ number of values.

points.label: Median
points.text: Middle value when arranged in order.

points.label: Mode
points.text: Value that appears most often.

slides.inSimpleWords: Mean is average, median is middle, mode is most common.

image.alt: Mean, Median, Mode — Data Handling and Presentation

slides.title: Calculating Mean

example.problem: Heights of 4 students: 140 cm, 145 cm, 135 cm, 150 cm. Find mean height.

slides.inSimpleWords: Add all values, divide by how many there are.

slides.title: Finding Median

example.problem: Test scores: 78, 82, 75, 90, 88. Find the median.
example.solution: Order: 75, 78, 82, 88, 90. Middle value = 82 (3rd of 5 values).

slides.inSimpleWords: Sort from smallest to largest, pick the middle.

slides.title: Identifying Mode

example.problem: Favorite colors: Blue, Red, Blue, Green, Blue, Red, Yellow. Find the mode.
example.solution: Blue appears 3 times, Red 2 times, Green 1, Yellow 1. Mode = Blue.

slides.inSimpleWords: Count which one repeats most; that's the mode.

slides.title: Finding Mean, Median, Mode
slides.storyContext: Vote counts: 8, 6, 4, 5, 7. Find mean, median, mode.

example.problem: Scores: 8, 6, 4, 5, 7. Find mean, median, mode.
example.solution: Mean = (8+6+4+5+7)÷5 = 30÷5 = 6. Median (ordered: 4,5,6,7,8) = 6. Mode = none (all appear once).

slides.inSimpleWords: Mean uses all values, median ignores outliers, mode shows preference.

image.alt: Finding Mean, Median, Mode — Data Handling and Presentation

slides.title: The Complete Journey
slides.storyContext: Meera shows Raj a poster: question → survey → tally → frequency table → chart → analysis.
slides.inSimpleWords: Data has a journey from question to understanding.

slides.title: Data Handling Steps

points.label: Step 1
points.text: Ask a clear question.

points.label: Step 2
points.text: Collect data (survey, observe, measure).

points.label: Step 3
points.text: Tally and create frequency table.

points.label: Step 4
points.text: Draw pictograph or bar chart.

points.label: Step 5
points.text: Analyze: find mean, median, mode; look for patterns.

slides.inSimpleWords: Follow steps from question to conclusion.

slides.title: Survey and Present
slides.storyContext: Meera asks Raj to survey 20 classmates on favorite games, make a bar chart, and find mean players per game.

points.label: Challenge
points.text: Collect data → Tally → Frequency table → Bar chart → Calculate mean.

slides.inSimpleWords: Go from survey to organized chart to statistical analysis.

image.alt: Survey and Present — Data Handling and Presentation

slides.title: Compare Two Datasets

example.problem: Survey 20 students on favorite meal (breakfast or lunch). Create two frequency tables, draw bar charts, compare means.
example.solution: Count votes for each meal type. Make tables side by side. Calculate mean for each. Compare which meal has higher average preference.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use data tools to compare and draw conclusions.

slides.title: Outlier Detective

example.problem: Scores: 10, 12, 11, 9, 50. Find mean, median, mode. Which is most helpful?
example.solution: Mean = 18.4 (pulled up by 50). Median = 11 (closer to reality). Mode = none. Median works best when there's an outlier.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different statistics reveal different truths.

slides.title: Data Handling Review
slides.storyContext: Raj and Meera review the complete data journey.

points.label: Collection
points.text: Ask clear questions, record carefully.

points.label: Organization
points.text: Frequency tables, pictographs, bar charts.

points.label: Analysis
points.text: Mean (average), Median (middle), Mode (most).

slides.inSimpleWords: Data tells stories when collected and presented clearly.

image.alt: Data Handling Review — Data Handling and Presentation

subject: Science
title: Raj's Nature Hike Classification
hook: Raj explores a nature trail and learns how scientists organize all living things.

slides.title: Nature Trail Discovery
slides.storyContext: During a hike, Raj spots plants, insects, birds, and mammals. Meera explains these are all organisms, but they're organized into different groups.
slides.inSimpleWords: Living things come in many different types.

image.alt: Nature Trail Discovery — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: What Makes Things Alive?
slides.storyContext: Meera shows Raj that all living things move, eat, grow, reproduce, and respond to their environment.

points.label: Characteristics
points.text: Growth, reproduction, response to environment, use of energy, homeostasis.

slides.inSimpleWords: Living things grow, move, reproduce, and respond to their world.

image.alt: What Makes Things Alive? — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: Is It Alive? Test

example.problem: Is a virus alive? It reproduces but needs a host cell. Is a crystal alive? It grows but doesn't reproduce.
example.solution: Virus: debate between scientists. Crystal: no—doesn't eat, move, or reproduce on its own. Both fail at least one 'alive' test.

slides.inSimpleWords: Living things must grow, eat, and reproduce all by themselves.

slides.title: Sorting Living Things
slides.storyContext: Meera takes out a chart. 'Scientists have five main groups for all life on Earth. Let's see how each one lives differently.'
slides.inSimpleWords: All life on Earth fits into five big groups.

slides.title: The Five Kingdoms
slides.storyContext: Raj learns the five kingdoms: Animals (move, eat), Plants (make own food), Fungi (decompose), Protists (single-celled mostly), Bacteria (tiny, everywhere).

example.problem: Classify these as animal, plant, or fungus: dog, rice, mushroom, tree, ant.
example.solution: Dog and ant are animals. Rice and tree are plants. Mushroom is fungus.

slides.inSimpleWords: Five major kingdoms organize all life on Earth.

image.alt: Kingdom Kingdoms — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: Kingdom Features

points.label: Animals
points.text: Eat food, move around, have many cells (dogs, insects, humans).

points.label: Plants
points.text: Make own food using sunlight, stay in place (trees, grass, flowers).

points.label: Fungi
points.text: Break down dead things (mushrooms, yeast, mold).

points.label: Protists
points.text: Mostly single-celled, simple (amoeba, algae).

points.label: Bacteria
points.text: Microscopic, everywhere (in soil, gut, water).

slides.inSimpleWords: Each kingdom has its own way of living.

slides.title: Inside the Animal Kingdom
slides.storyContext: Meera points to a bird and a butterfly. 'Notice: the bird has bones and a backbone. The butterfly doesn't. This is a big difference.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Animals split into two big groups by backbone.

slides.title: Vertebrates and Invertebrates
slides.storyContext: Raj notices the bird has bones (backbone), but the butterfly doesn't. Meera explains vertebrates have spines, invertebrates don't.

points.label: Vertebrates
points.text: Have backbone: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals.

points.label: Invertebrates
points.text: No backbone: insects, worms, crustaceans, mollusks, spiders.

slides.inSimpleWords: Vertebrates have backbones, invertebrates don't.

image.alt: Vertebrates and Invertebrates — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: Vertebrate Groups

points.label: Fish
points.text: Live in water, have gills, cold-blooded (goldfish, sharks).

points.label: Amphibians
points.text: Live part in water, part on land (frogs, toads).

points.label: Reptiles
points.text: Dry skin, cold-blooded (snakes, lizards, crocodiles).

points.label: Birds
points.text: Have feathers, lay eggs, warm-blooded (sparrows, eagles).

points.label: Mammals
points.text: Have hair, warm-blooded, feed milk to babies (dogs, whales, humans).

slides.inSimpleWords: Vertebrates are organized by how they survive.

slides.title: Animal Classification
slides.storyContext: Raj sorts animals he sees: sparrow (bird), lizard (reptile), beetle (insect), frog (amphibian), fish (fish).

example.problem: Classify: whale, snake, octopus, cow, eagle.
example.solution: Whale and cow are mammals. Snake is reptile. Octopus is mollusk. Eagle is bird.

slides.inSimpleWords: Groups share features: birds have feathers, fish have gills, mammals feed milk.

image.alt: Animal Classification — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: Plant Discoveries
slides.storyContext: The hikers see soft moss on a wet rock, fern fronds in the shade, and bright flowers in sunlight. 'All plants, but so different!' says Meera.
slides.inSimpleWords: Plants have a journey too: from simplest to most complex.

slides.title: Plants: Different Types
slides.storyContext: Meera points out mosses (no roots), ferns (have roots but no seeds), and flowering plants (have seeds and flowers).

points.label: Mosses
points.text: Simple plants, no roots or seeds, reproduce by spores.

points.label: Ferns
points.text: Have roots and leaves, reproduce by spores.

points.label: Seed Plants
points.text: Flowering and cone-bearing plants, reproduce by seeds.

slides.inSimpleWords: Plants get more complex: mosses → ferns → seed plants.

image.alt: Plants: Different Types — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: Moss and Fern Details

points.label: Moss
points.text: Soft, spongy, grows on damp places, no real roots.

points.label: Fern
points.text: Has thin roots, green leaflets, likes shade and moisture.

slides.inSimpleWords: Mosses are simple; ferns are in the middle.

slides.title: Seed Plants

points.label: Flowering Plants
points.text: Have flowers, colorful petals, fruit with seeds (roses, tomatoes).

points.label: Cone-bearing Plants
points.text: Have cones with seeds, usually evergreen (pine, spruce).

slides.inSimpleWords: Most plants we see have flowers or cones.

slides.title: Finding Plant Types
slides.storyContext: Raj identifies moss on a rock, fern in shade, and flowers in sunlight on the trail.

example.problem: You find three plants: one very simple on wet rock, one with leaves but no flowers, one with bright flowers. Classify each.
example.solution: Rock plant is moss. Leafy plant is fern. Flowering plant is a seed plant (flowering plant).

slides.inSimpleWords: Observe roots, seeds, and leaves to identify plant types.

image.alt: Finding Plant Types — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: The Hidden World
slides.storyContext: 'Look at this soil,' says Meera. 'Fungi, bacteria, tiny animals—billions of living things we can't see. All part of Earth's diversity.'
slides.inSimpleWords: Life exists at every scale, seen and unseen.

slides.title: Fungi and Microorganisms

points.label: Fungi
points.text: Break down dead plants and animals, help soil, many are visible (mushrooms, yeast).

points.label: Bacteria
points.text: Single-celled, everywhere, some help (yogurt, compost) and some cause disease.

points.label: Protists
points.text: Mostly single-celled, move in water, include algae that make oxygen.

slides.inSimpleWords: Fungi and bacteria are nature's recyclers.

slides.title: Microorganisms Around Us

example.problem: Name 3 helpful bacteria or fungi and 3 harmful ones.
example.solution: Helpful: yogurt bacteria, compost fungi, algae. Harmful: skin fungus, disease bacteria, food-spoiling fungi.

slides.inSimpleWords: Microbes are everywhere—some help us, some harm us.

slides.title: Connecting All Life
slides.storyContext: 'Every kingdom depends on the others,' explains Meera. 'Plants make oxygen, animals spread seeds, fungi decompose everything. It's all connected.'
slides.inSimpleWords: All five kingdoms work together in nature.

slides.title: How Nature Groups Organisms
slides.storyContext: Meera draws a tree: Kingdom splits into groups, groups split into more specific groups. 'It's like a family tree of all life,' she says.
slides.inSimpleWords: Scientists organize life by shared traits.

slides.title: Classification Hierarchy

points.label: Kingdom
points.text: Broadest group (Animals, Plants, Fungi, Protists, Bacteria).

points.label: Phylum
points.text: Major division within kingdom (Chordata for animals with backbone).

points.label: Class
points.text: Further grouping (Mammals, Birds, Reptiles within Chordata).

slides.inSimpleWords: Classification goes from broad to narrow.

slides.title: Classify Your Neighborhood
slides.storyContext: Meera challenges Raj to list 10 organisms he sees at home and classify each by kingdom and type.

points.label: Challenge
points.text: Note at least one animal, one plant, and one microorganism (like fungus bread mold).

slides.inSimpleWords: Look around and classify living things by their features.

image.alt: Classify Your Neighborhood — Diversity in the Living World

slides.title: Sort a Food Web

example.problem: In a garden: plants, grasshoppers, birds, fungus on dead leaves. Classify each into kingdom and type.
example.solution: Plants are in Kingdom Plantae. Grasshopper and bird are Kingdom Animalia (insect and bird). Fungus is Kingdom Fungi.

slides.inSimpleWords: Even food chains show the five kingdoms.

slides.title: Backbone vs. No Backbone

example.problem: List 5 vertebrates you know and 5 invertebrates. Draw a line down the middle.
example.solution: Vertebrates: dog, sparrow, fish, human, snake. Invertebrates: ant, worm, butterfly, crab, octopus.

slides.inSimpleWords: Practice spotting the backbone difference.

slides.title: Diversity Review
slides.storyContext: Raj and Meera finish the hike, appreciating Earth's incredible variety of life.

points.label: Kingdoms
points.text: Animals, Plants, Fungi, Protists, Bacteria.

points.label: Animals
points.text: Vertebrates (backbone) or Invertebrates (no backbone).

points.label: Plants
points.text: Mosses, Ferns, or Seed Plants (simple to complex).

slides.inSimpleWords: Life's diversity is organized by shared features.

image.alt: Diversity Review — Diversity in the Living World

subject: Science
title: Meera's Magnetic Adventure
hook: Meera discovers invisible forces when magnets attract and repel around her home.

slides.title: Magnetic Discovery
slides.storyContext: Meera picks up iron nails with a magnet. Raj asks, 'Why do they stick?' Meera explains that magnets have invisible pulling power.
slides.inSimpleWords: Magnets are objects with invisible pulling and pushing forces.

image.alt: Magnetic Discovery — Exploring Magnets

slides.title: What is a Magnet?
slides.storyContext: Meera shows different magnets: bar magnet, horseshoe magnet, electromagnet. They all attract iron and steel.

points.label: Magnet
points.text: Object with magnetic field; attracts iron and steel; has poles (north and south).

slides.inSimpleWords: A magnet attracts certain metals without touching them.

image.alt: What is a Magnet? — Exploring Magnets

slides.title: Types of Magnets

points.label: Bar Magnet
points.text: Rectangle shape, strong at ends (poles), used in experiments.

points.label: Horseshoe Magnet
points.text: Curved, poles at ends, stronger than bar magnet for same size.

points.label: Electromagnet
points.text: Coil of wire with electricity, can be switched on/off, used in doorbells and motors.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different magnet shapes have different strengths.

slides.title: Testing the Kitchen
slides.storyContext: Raj brings a magnet through the kitchen. 'Metal spoon—yes! Plastic cup—no! Aluminum foil—no! This is interesting!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Not all metal things are magnetic.

slides.title: Magnetic and Non-Magnetic
slides.storyContext: Meera tests objects: iron (attracted), aluminum foil (not attracted), steel (attracted), plastic (not attracted).

example.problem: Test these with a magnet: nail, rubber, coin, spoon, plastic bag.
example.solution: Nail and spoon attract (if metal). Rubber, coin, plastic bag don't attract.

slides.inSimpleWords: Iron, steel, and nickel are magnetic; most others are not.

image.alt: Magnetic and Non-Magnetic — Exploring Magnets

slides.title: What Can Be Magnetized?

points.label: Iron
points.text: Strongly attracted to magnets; can become a magnet itself.

points.label: Steel
points.text: Contains iron, also attracts to magnets.

points.label: Nickel and Cobalt
points.text: Weakly attracted to magnets.

points.label: Aluminum, Copper, Gold
points.text: Not attracted to ordinary magnets.

slides.inSimpleWords: Only certain metals respond to magnets.

slides.title: The Invisible Battle
slides.storyContext: Meera holds two bar magnets. 'Feel this—they push against each other! And now... they pull! Raj, swap one magnet's direction—now they push again!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Magnets can pull together or push apart.

slides.title: Magnetic Poles
slides.storyContext: Meera labels a bar magnet: North pole (N) and South pole (S). She notices they attract but opposite poles repel each other.

points.label: Poles
points.text: Every magnet has North and South poles. Opposite poles attract, like poles repel.

slides.inSimpleWords: N and S poles attract each other. N-N or S-S repel.

image.alt: Magnetic Poles — Exploring Magnets

slides.title: Attraction and Repulsion
slides.storyContext: Raj holds two bar magnets: N-S together (pull), N-N together (push). Meera explains the rule.

example.problem: Magnet A (N-S) and Magnet B (N-S). If A's north faces B's south, do they attract or repel?
example.solution: Opposite poles (N-S) attract each other.

slides.inSimpleWords: Opposite poles attract, same poles push away.

image.alt: Attraction and Repulsion — Exploring Magnets

slides.title: Earth Compass
slides.storyContext: Meera pulls out a compass and spins it. 'No matter which way I turn it, the needle always points north. Why?'
slides.inSimpleWords: Earth itself is a giant magnet.

slides.title: Earth's Magnetism

points.label: Earth is a Magnet
points.text: Liquid iron core creates Earth's magnetic field.

points.label: Compass
points.text: Needle aligns with Earth's field, north needle points to magnetic north.

points.label: Aurora
points.text: Colorful lights at poles caused by Earth's magnetic field.

slides.inSimpleWords: Earth itself is a giant magnet.

slides.title: The Pattern in Iron Filings
slides.storyContext: Meera spreads iron filings on paper above a magnet. 'Look, Raj—they line up! This shows the invisible shape of the magnet's power.'
slides.inSimpleWords: We can see the magnetic field with iron filings.

slides.title: Magnetic Field
slides.storyContext: Meera sprinkles iron filings around a magnet. The filings arrange in a pattern, showing the invisible magnetic field.

points.label: Magnetic Field
points.text: Invisible region around a magnet where magnetic force acts.

slides.inSimpleWords: Magnetic field is the invisible area where magnet's force works.

image.alt: Magnetic Field — Exploring Magnets

slides.title: Field Lines and Patterns

points.label: Pattern Shape
points.text: Field lines curve from north to south pole outside magnet, south to north inside.

points.label: Field Strength
points.text: Stronger at poles, weaker farther away.

slides.inSimpleWords: Field lines show how the magnet's force spreads.

slides.title: Observing Magnetic Fields
slides.storyContext: Iron filings create patterns around the magnet showing field lines radiating from poles.

example.problem: A magnet attracts a nail from 5 cm away. Is the nail in the magnetic field?
example.solution: Yes, the nail feels attraction from 5 cm away, so it's in the magnetic field region.

slides.inSimpleWords: If a magnet pulls something without touching, it's in the magnetic field.

image.alt: Observing Magnetic Fields — Exploring Magnets

slides.title: Testing Thickness
slides.storyContext: Meera puts paper, then glass, then water between a magnet and nail. 'Raj, the nail still moves! Does the magnet's force go through everything?'
slides.inSimpleWords: Magnetic force is special—it travels through barriers.

slides.title: Magnetic Force Through Materials

points.label: Through Paper
points.text: Magnetic force passes through easily, barely weakens.

points.label: Through Glass
points.text: Force passes through, slight weakening.

points.label: Through Water
points.text: Force passes through, weakens a little.

points.label: Through Plastic
points.text: Force passes through unchanged.

points.label: Through Iron
points.text: Force cannot pass; iron blocks it.

slides.inSimpleWords: Most materials let magnetic force through.

slides.title: Force Through Barriers

example.problem: You have a magnet and nail separated by 2 cm of paper. Will the nail attract to the magnet?
example.solution: Yes, magnetic force passes through paper almost unchanged. The nail will still move toward the magnet.

slides.inSimpleWords: Magnetic force is powerful enough to penetrate most barriers.

slides.title: Testing Different Materials

example.problem: Test these 5 materials with a magnet: iron nail, copper coin, aluminum foil, rubber, wooden pencil. Which attract?
example.solution: Only the iron nail attracts. Copper, aluminum, rubber, and wood do not attract to a magnet.

slides.inSimpleWords: Always test to discover what is magnetic.

slides.title: Magnets in Action
slides.storyContext: 'Magnets aren't just toys,' says Meera. 'Look around: doorbells use electromagnets, motors use them, even scrapyards use them to lift cars!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Magnets power everyday devices.

slides.title: Uses of Magnets

points.label: Electromagnets
points.text: Doorbells, motors, switches, medical scanners (MRI).

points.label: Permanent Magnets
points.text: Compasses, fridge magnets, speakers, hard drives.

points.label: Industrial
points.text: Scrapyards lift metal, mining, metal separation.

slides.inSimpleWords: Magnets are essential in technology and industry.

slides.title: Magnet Experiments
slides.storyContext: Meera challenges Raj to predict: will a magnet work through paper? Glass? Water? Test and explain.

points.label: Challenge
points.text: Magnetic force passes through paper and glass but weakens. Water also allows force to pass.

slides.inSimpleWords: Magnetic fields pass through many materials.

image.alt: Magnet Experiments — Exploring Magnets

slides.title: Design a Magnet Game

example.problem: Design a game using two magnets to move metal objects without touching them. Describe the rules.
example.solution: Place objects on paper above/below one magnet. Use another magnet to repel and attract them. Score points for moving to targets.

slides.inSimpleWords: Invisible forces can do real work.

slides.title: Predict Pole Interactions

example.problem: Three unlabeled magnets. Use a compass to find which pole is north on each, then predict attraction/repulsion.
example.solution: Compass needle points to south pole of magnet (north-seeking). Opposite poles attract, same repel.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use tools to discover hidden properties.

slides.title: Magnets Review
slides.storyContext: Meera and Raj explore everyday magnets: in compasses, door latches, magnetic stickers.

points.label: Basics
points.text: Magnets attract iron/steel via invisible poles (N and S).

points.label: Rules
points.text: Opposite poles attract, like poles repel, field passes through materials.

points.label: Uses
points.text: Compasses, electromagnets, motors, toys, separation tools.

slides.inSimpleWords: Magnets are forces that work through invisible fields.

image.alt: Magnets Review — Exploring Magnets
